newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese oil firms mull merging refining units.
newsitem.headline: Japanese oil firms mull merging refining units.

text.p: Two middle-ranked Japanese oil firms are mulling merging their refining divisions, which would create Japan"s biggest refiner and help them survive an impending shakeout in the industry.
Analysts said a merger would allow the two to cut costs dramatically, helping to soften the blow from high oil prices and a weak yen.
Showa Shell Sekiyu KK announced on Monday that it was considering merging its oil refining and distribution divisions with that of Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd.

"We have been exchanging information with Mitsubishi Oil on a possible merger. However, that"s just one of many options we have in mind," said Mitsuaki Nabetani, managing director of the Showa Shell, Japan"s fifth-biggest oil distributor.
"We have already been cooperating with Mitsubishi Oil in such fields as oil distribution and we are now studying if we can expand this cooperation further," he told a news briefing.

Sixth-ranked Mitsubishi Oil said on Sunday it was studying the possibility of a merger as one option to streamline its business operations, while a Showa Shell spokesman said it was being considered as a way to cut costs.
Neither company said when a final decision would be made.
Financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said on Sunday that the two firms may come up with a basic plan in May under which they would integrate their combined eight refineries in Japan.
If they merged their units, Showa Shell and Mitsubishi Oil would create Japan"s biggest oil refining company in terms of capacity, outpacing Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd.
The possible tie-up is seen as a bid to survive a likely industry-wide shakeout following deregulation of the oil products market and more global competition from Asian firms.

The financial situation of Japanese oil firms has worsened since the deregulation of oil product imports last April. The one-two punch of the weaker yen and higher oil prices have also dealt a heavy blow to their business.

Research firm Nikko Research Center said a merger of the two firms" refinery divisions would help them to cut costs substantially. But it did not expect a quick upturn in their business even with a merger of the units, as it saw the scope for a major recovery in the oil products market as limited.
"Oil sector shares have been sold on fears over damage to their business from the weaker yen, which boosts their costs, and sluggish domestic sales," a foreign brokerage trader said.

Mitsubishi Oil"s shares fell for a fourth straight session on Monday, depressed by its announcement on Friday that it will slip into the red in the year to March for the first time in 12 years, traders said.
Its shares ended down 15 yen at 508 yen, while Showa Shell lost eight yen to 822 yen on the Tokyo bourse.
Mitsubishi Oil said it saw a parent current loss for the year of 9.5 billion yen ($76.6 million), revising down its earlier forecast of eight billion yen ($64.5 million) profit.
Last month, Showa Shell also revised down its parent current profit outlook for calendar 1996 to 12 billion yen ($96.7 million) from its initial estimate of 20 billion yen ($161 million).
Showa Shell was created in 1985 through a merger of Shell Sekiyu and Showa Oil and is owned 50 percent by the Royal Dutch/Shell Group.
